title: Power Mapping and Analysis
subtitle: Understanding Influence Networks
description: Map formal and informal power structures. Identify key influencers and decision-makers.

content.overview: Power in government organizations exists in multiple forms - some visible, some hidden. Understanding the different types of power and how they operate is essential for navigating digital transformation initiatives. This module introduces the fundamental concepts of organizational power that underpin effective stakeholder engagement.

keyPoints.title: The Five Types of Organizational Power
characteristics: Legitimate power: Authority derived from formal position
Reward power: Ability to provide benefits or resources
Coercive power: Ability to impose negative consequences
Expert power: Influence based on knowledge or skills
Referent power: Influence based on respect and admiration
examples: Minister has legitimate power over the ministry
Budget controller has reward power through funding allocation
Audit department has coercive power through compliance enforcement
Chief Technology Officer has expert power in technical decisions
Respected senior advisor has referent power through credibility
keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: In DPI initiatives, you will encounter all five types. A successful digital transformation champion often needs to build expert and referent power when they lack legitimate, reward, or coercive power.

keyPoints.title: Formal vs Informal Power

formalPower.description: Power derived from official position, mandate, or organizational structure
formalPower.visibility: Usually visible in org charts, policies, and formal documents

informalPower.description: Power derived from relationships, expertise, or personal attributes
informalPower.visibility: Often invisible and must be discovered through observation and inquiry

keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: The person who can actually get things done in government is often not the person with the highest title. The Minister's executive assistant may have more practical influence than several directors.

patterns.description: Digital systems often redistribute power by changing who controls information
patterns.example: A new centralized database removes the gatekeeper power of department heads who previously controlled access to their siloed data
patterns.implication: Expect resistance from those whose power base depends on information asymmetry

patterns.pattern: Technical Expertise Creates New Power Centers
patterns.description: Those who understand new technology gain influence
patterns.example: IT staff who understand the new DPI platform become essential to everyone, gaining expert power
patterns.implication: Identify and cultivate relationships with technical experts early

patterns.description: Donor requirements or political mandates can override internal hierarchies
patterns.example: A presidential directive on digital ID gives the implementing team authority that bypasses normal ministry channels
patterns.implication: Understand the external forces that are reshaping internal power dynamics

content.keyInsight: In government digital transformation, formal power determines who can say yes, but informal power often determines what actually happens. You need to map both to succeed.

exercises.prompt: Think about a recent decision in your organization. Who had the formal authority to decide? Who actually influenced the outcome? What types of power did each person use?

content.overview: Formal power structures are the official framework of authority in an organization. While they don't tell the whole story, understanding them is essential for knowing who has legitimate decision-making authority and what channels you need to work through.

keyPoints.title: Reading Organizational Charts

techniques.how: Trace reporting lines from your target decision up to final approval authority
techniques.lookFor: Number of levels, span of control, matrix relationships
techniques.example: A DPI project approval may need to go through Department Head → Director General → Permanent Secretary → Minister

techniques.how: Understand how functions are organized and where boundaries lie
techniques.lookFor: Silos between technology and policy, between service delivery and administration
techniques.example: IT often sits under Administration while digital services may sit under Service Delivery - they may not coordinate

techniques.how: Identify where people report to multiple authorities
techniques.lookFor: Dotted-line relationships, project-based reporting, cross-functional teams
techniques.example: A DPI project manager may report to IT Director functionally but to the Minister's office for the specific initiative

keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: Government org charts often hide important structures - inter-ministerial committees, cabinet subcommittees, and coordination bodies that have significant power.

elements.description: Authority granted by law or regulation
examples: Ministry of ICT mandated to develop national IT policy
Data Protection Authority has legal power to audit systems
Central Bank has exclusive authority over payment systems
elements.importance: Legal mandates can override hierarchical authority - know who has statutory power

elements.description: Power delegated from higher authority, often with limits
examples: Director can approve spending up to $100K, above requires Secretary approval
Project manager authorized to sign vendor contracts under $50K
Department head can approve IT changes that don't affect other departments
elements.importance: Know the delegation limits - what can be decided at each level without escalation

elements.description: Sequence of approvals required for different decisions
examples: New system procurement: Technical review → Procurement → Legal → Finance → Executive
Policy change: Department → Inter-ministerial committee → Cabinet
Budget reallocation: Department → Planning → Finance → Treasury
elements.importance: Map the approval chain for your initiative - one missing approval can block everything

keyPoints.title: Budget Authority and Resource Control

aspects.description: Who decides how funds are distributed
key_questions: Who controls the budget for digital initiatives?
Is there a separate IT budget or is it distributed across departments?
Who can reallocate funds between line items?
What approval is needed for new spending categories?
aspects.example: The Ministry of Finance may have final say on any technology spending over $1M, regardless of which ministry is implementing

aspects.description: Who can commit the organization to spend
key_questions: What procurement rules apply to your initiative?
Who has signing authority at different spending levels?
Are there preferred vendor lists that constrain choices?
What role does central procurement play?
aspects.example: A DPI platform vendor selection may require going through Central Procurement Agency regardless of technical department preferences

aspects.description: Who controls staffing and skills allocation
key_questions: Who decides on hiring for the project?
Can staff be reassigned from other duties?
What approval is needed for external consultants?
aspects.example: The Civil Service Commission may need to approve any new technical positions, adding months to timeline

keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: In government, budget authority is often more powerful than organizational hierarchy. The person who controls the money may not be your boss, but they can determine your project's fate.

content.keyInsight: Formal power structures tell you who can officially approve, block, or fund your initiative. Master this map before trying to navigate the informal networks - you need to know which formal hurdles must be cleared.

exercises.prompt: For a current or planned DPI initiative, map the formal approval chain. Who needs to sign off? What budget authorities are involved? What legal mandates affect the initiative? Create a visual diagram showing the formal power structure.

content.overview: Informal power networks are the hidden wiring of organizations. While org charts show formal structure, real influence flows through relationships, trust, and expertise. Understanding these networks is often the difference between initiatives that succeed and those that stall despite having official approval.

categories.description: Influence derived from personal connections and trust
manifestations: Family or social connections outside work
Alumni networks from same university or training program
categories.example: The Deputy Director who went to university with the Minister has more real influence than his title suggests
categories.inGovernmentContext: Government careers are long - relationships built over decades create invisible channels of influence

categories.description: Influence derived from unique knowledge or skills
manifestations: Only person who understands the legacy system
Institutional memory of past failures and successes
categories.example: The mid-level IT manager who maintained the tax system for 15 years knows where all the integration points are - no decision can be made without consulting her
categories.inGovernmentContext: In digital transformation, technical experts become powerful because leaders depend on their knowledge to make decisions

categories.description: Influence derived from proximity to decision-makers
manifestations: Executive assistant who controls the calendar
Driver who has daily private time with the Minister
IT support person who has access to everyone's systems
categories.example: The Minister's personal assistant decides who gets on the calendar - she effectively controls access to the most powerful person in the ministry
categories.inGovernmentContext: Never underestimate support staff - they often control access to the people you need to reach

categories.description: Influence derived from connections across organizational boundaries
manifestations: Person who knows counterparts in every ministry
Person who bridges technical and political worlds
Someone with international connections and exposure
categories.example: The policy advisor who previously worked at the World Bank knows everyone in the donor community and can facilitate or block international support
categories.inGovernmentContext: Cross-boundary connectors are invaluable for DPI initiatives that require coordination across ministries and with external partners

methods.description: Watch who talks to whom, who gets consulted, who people defer to
indicators: Who do people look at when a decision needs to be made?
Who gets pulled into meetings unexpectedly?
Whose opinion do people seek before acting?
Who can get the Secretary on the phone immediately?
Who do people complain to when things go wrong?

methods.description: Ask questions to understand influence patterns
questions: If you needed to get this approved quickly, who would you talk to?
Who really understands how things work around here?
Who should I definitely not surprise with this proposal?
Who has the Minister's ear on technology issues?
Who would you want on your side if this got controversial?

methods.description: Study past decisions to understand influence patterns
questions: How did the last major IT project get approved?
Who championed successful initiatives?
Who blocked proposals that failed?
What alliances formed around previous controversies?
Who has survived multiple leadership changes?

insights.description: Government officials are cautious about who they trust
insights.implication: Building informal power takes time - quick wins matter less than consistent reliability
insights.example: After delivering three projects on time and under budget, you become the person the Secretary calls for honest assessments

insights.description: An introduction from a trusted person carries weight
insights.implication: Find sponsors who can vouch for you to key stakeholders
insights.example: The Director trusts the policy advisor, and the policy advisor vouches for you - now the Director gives you the benefit of the doubt

insights.description: One betrayal of confidence can destroy years of relationship building
insights.implication: Never share information inappropriately, never surprise someone who trusted you
insights.example: Leaking a confidential concern to the press will permanently close doors that took years to open

content.keyInsight: Formal authority can command compliance, but informal power generates commitment. The person who can actually mobilize support for your DPI initiative may not be the person with the biggest title.

exercises.prompt: Identify three people in your organization who have significant informal power without corresponding formal authority. What is the source of their influence? How might you build relationships with them?

content.overview: Power mapping is the systematic process of identifying, analyzing, and visualizing stakeholders and their influence relationships. This module provides practical tools and frameworks for creating power maps that inform your engagement strategy.

keyPoints.title: The Power-Interest Grid
keyPoints.description: A 2x2 matrix for categorizing stakeholders by their power level and interest in your initiative

quadrants.label: Key Players
examples: Minister responsible for digital transformation
Permanent Secretary of implementing ministry
Director of IT who must deliver the project
quadrants.tactics: Regular updates, involvement in key decisions, early warning of issues, address concerns promptly

quadrants.label: Keep Satisfied
examples: Minister of Finance who controls budget but doesn't focus on technology
Cabinet Secretary who approves major decisions but delegates details
Attorney General who must sign off on legal aspects
quadrants.tactics: Brief, targeted updates on matters requiring their action, no surprises, clear asks when needed

quadrants.label: Keep Informed
quadrants.strategy: Keep engaged as they can influence others
examples: Civil society groups interested in digital rights
Technical staff who will use the system
Junior reformers who champion the initiative
quadrants.tactics: Regular communication, seek their input, leverage their enthusiasm to build momentum

quadrants.label: Monitor
quadrants.strategy: Minimal effort but watch for changes
examples: Departments not directly affected
Staff in unrelated functions
External parties with peripheral interest
quadrants.tactics: Basic awareness, monitor for changes in interest or power that would require reclassification

keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: In government, power and interest levels can shift rapidly with political changes, scandals, or new priorities. Review and update your grid regularly.

keyPoints.title: Influence Mapping
keyPoints.description: Visualizing who influences whom to understand indirect pathways to decision-makers

steps.how: Be specific about what decision you're trying to influence
steps.example: Approval of $5M budget for national digital ID pilot

steps.how: Who directly advises or informs the decision-maker?
steps.example: Minister's policy advisor, IT Director, Budget Director, external consultants
Technical staff who brief the IT Director, donor representatives who advise the policy team

steps.how: Show relationships and note their nature (formal reporting, informal trust, etc.)
steps.example: Solid line for reporting relationships, dotted for advisory, thick lines for strong trust

steps.how: Find multiple routes to reach the decision-maker
steps.example: Direct: through IT Director. Indirect: through donor partner who has Minister's ear

visualElements: Colors indicate support level (green = supporter, red = blocker, yellow = neutral)

keyPoints.title: Relationship Mapping
keyPoints.description: Understanding the quality and history of relationships between key players

dimensions.importance: High trust relationships are channels for influence, distrust relationships are barriers
Frequent communication indicates working relationships that can be leveraged

dimensions.range: Long positive history to recent conflict
dimensions.importance: Past conflicts may create lasting barriers; shared successes create goodwill
Dependencies create opportunities for exchange and negotiation

keyPoints.example: The IT Director and Budget Director have a tense relationship from a previous failed project. Going through Budget to reach IT will not work - need an alternative pathway.
keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: Government relationship maps often reflect decades of history. A conflict from ten years ago may still poison a relationship today.

keyPoints.title: Coalition Mapping
keyPoints.description: Identifying existing alliances and potential coalitions

elements.description: Groups that already work together and share interests
examples: The modernizers: IT Director, young policy advisors, donor partners
The traditionalists: senior civil servants, union representatives, risk-averse managers
The budget guardians: Finance ministry, audit office, procurement authority

elements.description: Stakeholders who might align if brought together
examples: Citizens groups and anti-corruption advocates both want transparency
Service delivery departments and IT both want efficient systems
Finance ministry and reform advocates both want to reduce fraud
Centralization vs. local autonomy
Speed vs. thoroughness
Innovation vs. risk management

keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: Understanding existing coalitions helps you identify natural allies and avoid stepping into ongoing conflicts you don't understand.

content.keyInsight: A power map is not just a diagram - it's a strategic tool. The purpose is not to document relationships but to identify the most effective pathways to achieve your goals.

exercises.prompt: Create a power-interest grid for your current DPI initiative. Place at least 10 stakeholders on the grid. For each one, note: their source of power, their primary interest, and your current relationship quality. Then create an influence map showing how these stakeholders connect to each other.

content.overview: Not everyone with a title actually makes decisions. This module focuses on identifying who really decides - distinguishing between nominal decision-makers and actual decision-makers, and understanding the roles of gatekeepers and veto players.

keyPoints.title: Nominal vs. Actual Decision-Makers

nominalDecisionMaker.description: The person who formally approves or signs off
characteristics: Has the title and formal authority
Signs the documents
Is publicly accountable for the decision
May or may not have deeply analyzed the issue
nominalDecisionMaker.example: The Minister signs the contract, but she relies entirely on her advisors' recommendations

actualDecisionMaker.description: The person whose judgment determines the outcome
characteristics: Does the actual analysis or forms the judgment
Their recommendation is almost always followed
May not have formal authority but has effective authority
Often operates behind the scenes
actualDecisionMaker.example: The policy advisor reviews all technology proposals and his recommendation has been followed in every case for the past three years

identificationQuestions: Who prepares the brief or recommendation that gets approved?
When was the last time the nominal decision-maker rejected the recommendation?
If there's disagreement, whose view prevails?
Who does the nominal decision-maker consult before deciding?
keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: In government, the actual decision-maker is often one or two levels below the person who signs. Ministers and senior officials frequently rubber-stamp well-prepared recommendations.

keyPoints.title: Gatekeepers
keyPoints.description: People who control access to decision-makers or information flow

types.role: Control who gets time with the decision-maker
examples: Executive assistants who manage calendars
Chiefs of staff who filter requests
Security personnel who control physical access
types.strategy: Build positive relationships, respect their role, make their job easier

types.role: Control what information reaches the decision-maker
examples: Staff who prepare briefing documents
Advisors who summarize technical reports
Communications teams who manage messaging
types.strategy: Ensure your information is accurate and complete, build trust so your inputs aren't filtered out

types.role: Control the procedures required for decisions
examples: Procurement officers who determine bidding requirements
Legal counsel who must approve contracts
Finance officers who verify budget availability
types.strategy: Understand their requirements early, comply fully, build relationships so they prioritize your requests

keyPoints.inGovernmentContext: Gatekeepers in government often have more power than their titles suggest. An unfriendly procurement officer can delay your project for months through strict interpretation of rules.

keyPoints.title: Veto Players
keyPoints.description: People who can block a decision even if they cannot approve it
characteristics: May not be in the direct approval chain
Have authority to stop or delay the process
Often have specific functional concerns
Their opposition must be addressed or circumvented

commonVetoPlayers.example: Attorney General's office refuses to approve digital signature framework citing legal uncertainty

commonVetoPlayers.vetoGround: Budget availability, fiscal rules, value for money
commonVetoPlayers.example: Treasury blocks project despite ministry approval because funds aren't in the right budget category
Data Commissioner raises concerns about biometric collection that must be resolved before proceeding
Intelligence service objects to cloud hosting of citizen data

commonVetoPlayers.vetoGround: Worker impact, job security, working conditions
commonVetoPlayers.example: Civil service union threatens industrial action if automation threatens jobs

keyPoints.strategy: Identify veto players early, engage them before they become obstacles, address their concerns proactively, find ways to give them wins within your project.

patterns.description: Decision requires agreement from multiple parties
patterns.indicators: Extensive consultation, inter-ministerial committees, long timelines
patterns.approach: Invest in building broad coalition, address all concerns, patient engagement

patterns.description: Senior leader makes decisions with minimal consultation
patterns.indicators: Quick decisions, top-down communication, limited debate
patterns.approach: Focus on reaching and convincing the key decision-maker directly

patterns.description: Decision follows established procedures regardless of individuals
patterns.indicators: Formal committees, standardized criteria, documented procedures
patterns.approach: Master the process, meet all criteria, navigate procedural requirements

patterns.description: Decisions made rapidly in response to urgent situations
patterns.indicators: Ad hoc meetings, bypassed procedures, rapid implementation
patterns.approach: Be ready with solutions when crises create windows of opportunity

content.keyInsight: Finding the real decision-maker is detective work. Don't assume the person with the title makes the decision - trace back from past decisions to understand who actually determines outcomes.

exercises.prompt: For a decision you need, identify: (1) the nominal decision-maker, (2) who you believe is the actual decision-maker and why, (3) all gatekeepers you must navigate, and (4) potential veto players who could block the decision. What is your strategy for each?

content.overview: Beyond formal decision-makers lie the influencers - people who shape opinions, provide trusted advice, and can move positions without formal authority. This module focuses on identifying these critical players and understanding how to work with them.

categories.description: People whose judgment is sought and followed by decision-makers
characteristics: Have the decision-maker's confidence and trust
Are consulted before major decisions
Their opinion carries significant weight
May not have formal role in the decision process
examples: Long-serving civil servant who has seen everything
External consultant with strong track record
Party ally who provides political counsel
Technical expert the Minister relies on
categories.inGovernmentContext: Ministers often have a small circle of trusted advisors they consult on everything - identifying these people is crucial

categories.description: People whose views shape broader organizational opinion
characteristics: Respected by peers and subordinates
Their positions influence others' positions
Often vocal in meetings and discussions
Seen as thought leaders on certain topics
examples: Senior technical architect whose views on technology are widely respected
Department head known for sound judgment
Reform champion who inspires others
categories.inGovernmentContext: If the opinion leader in a department opposes your initiative, you'll face resistance even with top-level approval

categories.description: People who connect different groups and translate between them
characteristics: Trusted by multiple groups
Can translate technical to policy language and vice versa
Move easily between different departments or levels
Often facilitate negotiations and compromises
examples: Policy advisor with technical background
Former ministry staff now at donor organization
Career civil servant known to everyone across government
categories.inGovernmentContext: DPI initiatives often require coordination across many ministries - bridge builders are invaluable for making these connections

categories.description: People with significant influence that isn't immediately visible
characteristics: Operate behind the scenes
May have historical or external relationships that create influence
Often underestimated based on their formal position
Their opposition can quietly kill initiatives
examples: Retired official who still advises current leadership
Business leader with political connections
Family member of a key decision-maker
Party official without government role
categories.inGovernmentContext: In many governments, political parties, business interests, or family connections create invisible power structures

methods.description: Trace back how previous decisions were made
questions: Who was consulted before the decision?
Whose arguments carried the day?
Who seemed to know what would happen before it was announced?
Who was brought into the room at critical moments?

methods.description: Observe who communicates with whom and how
questions: Who does the decision-maker call or meet with regularly?
Whose calls are always taken?
Who is copied on important emails?
Who is in the unofficial chat groups?

methods.description: Ask trusted contacts about influence patterns
questions: Who should I really talk to about this?
Who does the Minister actually listen to?
Who would you want supporting this if it got controversial?
Who makes things happen around here?

signals: Who do people look at when a decision is being made?
Whose reaction do people watch for?

strategies.description: Bring influencers in before positions harden
strategies.approach: Share early thinking, ask for input, make them feel ownership
strategies.example: Before finalizing the DPI architecture, share draft with the technical opinion leader and genuinely incorporate feedback

strategies.approach: Regular informal contact, sharing useful information, being helpful without always asking for something
strategies.example: Send the trusted advisor interesting articles on digital transformation, have coffee occasionally without asking for anything

strategies.description: Use one influencer to reach another
strategies.approach: Identify who influences your target influencer, build relationship there first
strategies.example: The Minister's trusted advisor respects the University professor - get the professor on board first

strategies.approach: Address concerns seriously, give them face-saving ways to change position
strategies.example: The opinion leader was skeptical of digital ID - address his privacy concerns and let him claim credit for improved privacy features

content.keyInsight: Influencers are force multipliers. A single supporter with real influence is worth more than many supporters without influence. Invest your relationship-building energy where it will have the most impact.

exercises.prompt: Identify the key influencers for your initiative. For each, categorize their type, assess your current relationship (strong/weak/none), and develop a specific strategy for engagement. Who is the highest-priority influencer you don't yet have a relationship with?

content.overview: Every digital transformation initiative faces resistance. Understanding who might block your initiative, why they resist, and how to address their concerns is essential for success. This module examines the anatomy of resistance and strategies for managing blockers.

categories.description: Initiative threatens someone's power, budget, or status
manifestations: Loss of control over information or resources
Obsolescence of current skills or role
examples: Department head who currently controls the data that will be shared
IT staff whose manual processes will be automated
Vendor whose contract will not be renewed
categories.approach: Understand what they're losing, find ways to compensate or create new value for them

categories.description: Real problems or risks that haven't been adequately addressed
examples: Data Protection Commissioner worried about biometric collection
Finance officer doubting cost estimates
Technical expert seeing architectural flaws
categories.approach: Listen seriously, address concerns genuinely, improve your proposal based on valid criticism

manifestations: Reluctance to invest energy in another initiative
Wait and see whether this will last
examples: Staff who saw three previous IT projects fail
Manager whose team is already overwhelmed
Civil servant who has outlasted many reform initiatives
categories.approach: Acknowledge past experiences, differentiate your approach, start with small wins to build credibility

categories.description: Fundamental disagreement with the direction or approach
manifestations: Philosophical objections to centralization or digitization
Political opposition to the sponsoring government
Belief that technology is not the answer
examples: Privacy advocate who opposes any national ID
Civil society group suspicious of government surveillance
Opposition politician who will attack any government initiative
categories.approach: Engage respectfully, find common ground where possible, work around if no accommodation is possible

manifestations: Public criticism or statements against the initiative
behaviors.advantage: At least it's visible and can be addressed directly
behaviors.danger: Can build momentum and attract other opponents
Difficult to address because it's not acknowledged

behaviors.description: Using rules and processes to delay or block
manifestations: Insisting on strict interpretation of regulations
behaviors.advantage: Plausibly deniable as just doing their job
behaviors.danger: Very effective at killing momentum through delay

manifestations: Setting up the initiative to fail
behaviors.danger: Can cause serious damage, hard to trace

strategies.description: Turn blockers into supporters through genuine engagement
strategies.when: When concerns are legitimate and person is open to dialogue
how: Listen to understand their real concerns
Address concerns genuinely in your approach
Give them a role that makes them invested
Provide face-saving way to change position
strategies.example: The IT Director was blocking because he wasn't consulted - bring him into the design team and incorporate his expertise

strategies.description: Reduce the blocker's ability to influence others
strategies.when: When blocker is unreasonable and cannot be converted
how: Demonstrate their concerns are not widely shared
Create alternative channels that bypass them
strategies.example: The budget officer blocks everything - build relationship with Finance Director who can override

strategies.description: Use higher authority to overcome resistance
strategies.when: When you have clear mandate and blocker lacks authority to stop you
how: Escalate to decision-maker with authority over blocker
Get explicit directive that clarifies authority
strategies.example: Department head refuses to share data - get cabinet directive requiring data sharing

strategies.description: Find alternative paths that avoid the blocker
strategies.when: When direct confrontation is not worth the cost
how: Restructure scope to avoid their domain
strategies.example: Start with pilot in supportive ministry rather than fighting resistant ministry for initial implementation

strategies.when: When blocker is temporary or situation will change
how: Watch for changes in leadership or priorities
Build support for when opportunity arrives
strategies.example: The resistant Secretary is retiring in six months - build relationships with likely successor

content.keyInsight: Blockers are not just obstacles - they're sources of information about what could go wrong. The concerns that drive resistance often identify real problems that need to be addressed. Even if you disagree with the blocker, understanding their perspective makes your initiative stronger.

exercises.prompt: Identify the top three potential blockers for your initiative. For each, analyze: (1) their source of resistance, (2) the type of blocking behavior you expect, (3) your strategy for managing them, and (4) what you would do if that strategy fails. Is there a blocker you might be able to convert into a supporter?

content.overview: This module brings together all the concepts from the course into a practical process for building, using, and maintaining your power map. A good power map is a living strategic tool that guides your stakeholder engagement throughout your initiative.

process.description: Be specific about what decision or outcome you're trying to influence
questions: What exactly needs to be decided?
What is the timeline for this decision?
What criteria will be used?
What is the formal process?
process.example: Cabinet approval of $10M digital identity pilot by end of fiscal year, evaluated on cost, risk, and alignment with government priorities

process.description: Brainstorm everyone who might affect or be affected by the decision
process.tip: Cast a wide net initially - you can filter later

process.description: For each stakeholder, assess key dimensions
dimensions: Power: How much can they affect the outcome?
Interest: How much do they care?
Position: Are they supporter, neutral, or opposed?
Concerns: What are their key concerns?
Relationship: What is your current relationship?

process.description: Determine how to reach key decision-makers
questions: What is the most direct path to the decision-maker?
What alternative paths exist?
Who can open doors for you?
Where are the bottlenecks?

applications.description: Allocate your time and energy based on the map
guidance: Focus first on high-power, high-interest stakeholders
Don't ignore high-power, low-interest stakeholders - keep them informed
Address blockers based on your management strategy

applications.description: Tailor your communication to each stakeholder
considerations: What messages resonate with each stakeholder?
What level of detail is appropriate?
What concerns should you address proactively?

principles: Address blocker concerns before they escalate
Time high-stakes conversations for maximum impact

applications.description: Monitor stakeholder positions and relationship development
metrics: Movement from opposed to neutral to supportive

practices.frequency: Weekly during active engagement, monthly otherwise
questions: Have any stakeholder positions changed?
Have new stakeholders emerged?
Have relationships shifted?
Are your strategies working?

practices.description: Events that require immediate map revision

elements: Lines showing relationships (solid = formal, dotted = informal)

mistakes.description: Creating the map once and not updating it
mistakes.remedy: Build regular review into your routine

mistakes.description: Focusing only on org charts and official roles
mistakes.remedy: Always map both formal and informal power

mistakes.consequence: Blockers become more entrenched and effective
mistakes.remedy: Engage blockers early with clear strategy

mistakes.description: Expecting quick results from relationship investment
mistakes.remedy: Start relationship building early, be patient

mistakes.description: Not sharing stakeholder intelligence with your team
mistakes.consequence: Team members make mistakes you could prevent
mistakes.remedy: Share appropriate parts of the map with team members who need it

content.keyInsight: A power map is only valuable if it changes your behavior. The goal is not a pretty diagram - it's a strategic tool that helps you make better decisions about where to invest your relationship-building energy and how to navigate the path to your goals.

exercises.prompt: Build a complete power map for your current or upcoming DPI initiative. Include: (1) a stakeholder register with at least 15 stakeholders, (2) an influence diagram showing key relationships, (3) a prioritized engagement plan for your top 5 stakeholders, and (4) a strategy for managing your most significant blocker. Schedule a weekly review session in your calendar and identify what triggers should prompt an immediate map update.

targetAudience: DPI advisors, government IT directors, policy coordinators working on digital transformation
